case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Federal Election Campaign Act’s limits on coordinated expenditures by political parties with their candidates violate the First Amendment, and whether (or how) existing Supreme Court precedent upholding such limits—especially Colorado II—should control or be revisited.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) coordinated party expenditure limits (the statutory caps on party committee spending made in coordination with a candidate), challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (NRSC and aligned party committees) argue that FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits unconstitutionally restrict core political speech and associational activity by political parties and candidates. They contend that Colorado II should not foreclose relief because later doctrinal developments in campaign-finance/First Amendment law have undermined Colorado II’s reasoning, and that coordinated spending by parties should be treated more like protected political speech than like a regulable quid-pro-quo contribution. They also press a practical/systemic argument: current law weakens parties relative to outside groups, and removing the limits would better allow parties to engage in direct, central campaign speech and coordination. In response to concerns about circumvention of contribution limits, petitioners emphasize the continued existence of other ‘guardrails’ (other contribution limits and anti-circumvention rules), while attempting to keep the case narrowly focused on party coordinated-expenditure caps rather than broader contribution-limit validity.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (FEC and supporting parties/intervenors) argue that the challenge is controlled by FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II), which upheld coordinated party expenditure limits as a permissible anti-circumvention measure because coordinated spending functions like a contribution that can be used to evade candidate contribution limits and facilitate quid-pro-quo corruption or its appearance. They stress that lower courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent (Rodriguez de Quijas), and that petitioners’ ‘as-applied’ framing cannot succeed where it repackages the same factual and legal premises the Supreme Court already considered when rejecting a facial challenge. Respondents further question petitioners’ policy premise that invalidation would strengthen parties rather than shift influence in ways that could weaken party institutions or amplify large-donor leverage through party conduits. They also highlight that petitioners cannot reliably promise that other campaign-finance limits will remain in place (given petitioners’ broader constitutional objections elsewhere), which matters because the asserted safety of striking these limits depends on those remaining constraints.
key_precedents: FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II), 533 U.S. 431 (2001)
Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477 (1989)
Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, 597 U.S. 507 (2022)
Thompson v. Marietta Education Association, 972 F.3d 809 (6th Cir. 2020)
Limbach v. Hooven & Allison Co., 466 U.S. 353 (1984)
California Medical Association v. FEC, 453 U.S. 182 (1981)
California Water Service Co. v. City of Redding, 304 U.S. 252 (1938)
Mariani v. United States (referenced for legislative-fact findings in FECA certification procedure), 212 F.3d 761 (3d Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas forcefully argues that “anti-circumvention” can become an untethered prophylaxis that dilutes core First Amendment protection by relabeling speech as contribution-like, but that concern is answered here by the narrow, coordination-specific holding of Colorado II: when party spending is made in concert with the candidate, it functions as a conduit for targeted support and is therefore regulable under “closely drawn” scrutiny tied to quid pro quo corruption and its appearance. Justice Kagan and Justice Alito rightly emphasize Rodriguez de Quijas: whatever doctrinal “tension” later independent-expenditure cases create, it is not our role to treat Colorado II as implicitly overruled, especially in a complex statutory scheme with reliance and administrability implications. Petitioners’ claim that other “guardrails” will prevent evasion is speculative and invites piecemeal destabilization of FECA’s integrated structure; minimalism counsels deciding only that § 30116(d) remains constitutional under controlling precedent. I therefore adhere to Colorado II on the narrow ground that coordinated party expenditures may be capped to prevent circumvention of valid candidate contribution limits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s reliance on Rodriguez de Quijas and Colorado II is the strongest point for Respondents, but it does not answer the antecedent question whether Colorado II itself is faithful to the First Amendment’s text and original public meaning. Calling coordinated party expenditures “contribution-like” is a doctrinal relabeling that permits Congress to cap core political speech and association based on a broad anti-circumvention rationale, untethered to the only historically grounded corruption interest—quid pro quo—as I understand it. Justice Kagan’s coherence/administrability concern is essentially a policy defense of FECA’s architecture; it cannot supply constitutional authority to burden protected political advocacy, nor can reliance interests justify retaining a rule that lacks originalist footing. Because § 30116(d) directly restrains party speech made with and about candidates, and because Colorado II’s functionalist approach dilutes First Amendment protection without adequate constitutional grounding, I would overrule it and hold the provision unconstitutional.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s original-meaning critique forcefully challenges Colorado II’s premise, but under my stare decisis approach it is not enough, by itself, to discard a directly controlling decision in a dense, reliance-heavy regulatory scheme. Chief Justice Roberts correctly invokes Rodriguez de Quijas: whatever doctrinal “tension” later cases may create regarding independent expenditures, we are not free to treat Colorado II’s coordination holding as implicitly overruled, especially where coordination is the feature that makes the spending functionally contribution-like and thus subject to closely drawn limits. Thomas also argues that “anti-circumvention” is an amorphous license, but here the anticircumvention rationale is tethered to preserving valid base contribution caps against a predictable conduit problem—petitioners’ proposed “guardrails” are too speculative to answer that practical risk. Absent a developed showing that Colorado II is unworkable or irreconcilable with subsequent holdings on coordinated spending, I would adhere to it and uphold § 30116(d).

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that coordinated party expenditures are core political advocacy and that an “anti-circumvention” rationale can become an overbroad prophylaxis untethered to quid pro quo corruption; but coordination is precisely what converts spending into a functional contribution, because it gives the candidate control or substantial influence over the use of funds and thus creates both quid pro quo risks and a ready conduit to evade base candidate limits. Colorado II directly addressed this coordination problem and sustained these caps under closely drawn scrutiny, and—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s reliance on Rodriguez de Quijas—later doctrinal shifts about independent expenditures do not implicitly overrule a precedent squarely about coordinated spending. From a pragmatic, real-world perspective, striking the caps would predictably increase the leverage of large donors to buy access by routing money through party committees aligned with the candidate, undermining public confidence and burdening voters with the least power. Petitioners’ “guardrails” argument is too contingent to justify dismantling a targeted anti-circumvention rule that Congress designed to preserve the integrity of contribution limits.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to warn that an “anti-circumvention” rationale can become an unbounded license to suppress political speech, but that critique does not fit § 30116(d) as construed in Colorado II, which treated coordinated party spending as contribution-like because coordination gives the candidate practical control and creates a concrete conduit for quid-pro-quo deals and evasion of valid base limits. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, Rodriguez de Quijas matters here: whatever later cases say about independent expenditures, they do not authorize us to treat Colorado II’s coordination-specific holding as silently overruled, especially in an integrated statutory scheme where coherence and administrability are central. Petitioners’ “other guardrails” pitch underscores that severing this provision would destabilize FECA’s interlocking limits and invite line-drawing and evasion litigation rather than a narrow, textual fix. If petitioners want us to revisit the constitutional foundation of Colorado II, they must squarely seek overruling and carry the stare decisis burden; on this record, I would apply controlling precedent and uphold the statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas rightly presses that “anti-circumvention” cannot become a roving license to suppress political speech untethered from the First Amendment’s original meaning, and that is the hardest point for respondents. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito emphasize, Colorado II did not rest on a free-floating prophylaxis; it treated coordination as the constitutionally relevant fact that makes party spending function as a contribution-like transfer of value to the candidate and a conduit for evading valid base limits—an interest our cases have tied to quid pro quo corruption and its appearance. Rodriguez de Quijas, which Roberts invokes, counsels that we apply directly controlling precedent rather than deem it implicitly displaced by later independent-expenditure decisions addressing a different category of spending. On my separation-of-powers approach, the narrower and more principled course is to follow Colorado II here; if it is to be overruled, that should occur on a full stare decisis showing, not by indirection in a case squarely covered by existing law.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that “anti-circumvention” can become an unmoored license to burden core party advocacy, but Colorado II already made the constitutionally relevant, administrable distinction: coordination gives the candidate effective control and converts the spending into a contribution-like conduit tied to quid-pro-quo/appearance and evasion risks. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Rodriguez de Quijas counsels that we may not treat later independent-expenditure cases as implicitly overruling a square holding on coordinated party expenditures, especially in a complex regulatory area with substantial reliance interests. Justice Kagan’s coherence/workability concern reinforces that striking only § 30116(d) would destabilize FECA’s integrated backstops and invite line-drawing litigation over “guardrails” that petitioners cannot guarantee. On my institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, Thomas’s originalist critique does not supply a stare decisis basis strong enough to reopen and overrule Colorado II in this posture.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press that “anti-circumvention” cannot become an amorphous, policy-driven warrant to suppress political advocacy, and an originalist account of the First Amendment would likely resist broad prophylaxis. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Colorado II did not adopt a free-floating rationale; it treated spending coordinated with a candidate as contribution-like because coordination supplies something of value to the candidate and creates a concrete conduit for evading valid base contribution limits, which fits within our quid-pro-quo/appearance framework and triggers only “closely drawn” review. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, later independent-expenditure cases (Citizens United, McCutcheon) do not authorize us to treat that coordination-specific holding as silently overruled, and petitioners have not made the kind of targeted stare decisis showing (unworkability or doctrinal irreconcilability) that would justify discarding Colorado II here. The statute’s narrow focus on coordinated party spending also answers Thomas’s breadth concern in a way that is consistent with a textualist, precedent-respecting approach.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s originalist critique forcefully warns that “anti-circumvention” can become an untethered license to ration political speech, but here the rationale is not free-floating: as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Colorado II specifically treated candidate-coordinated party spending as functionally contribution-like because coordination creates a conduit for large, targeted support and thus a concrete quid-pro-quo/appearance and evasion risk. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, I agree with Justice Alito that later independent-expenditure cases cannot be read to silently displace a square holding about coordinated spending, especially in an integrated statutory scheme where administrability and reliance matter. Petitioners’ “other guardrails” position remains procedurally unstable and practically contingent, and—as Justice Sotomayor notes—would predictably invite circumvention pressure that undermines the remaining contribution limits and public confidence. Nothing in Thomas’s argument, on this record and posture, supplies a stare decisis justification strong enough to overrule or narrow Colorado II in a way that invalidates § 30116(d).

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado II squarely upheld FECA’s caps on coordinated party expenditures on the ground that coordinated party spending functions like a contribution and is a permissible anti-circumvention measure to protect candidate contribution limits and prevent quid-pro-quo corruption or its appearance. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts (and absent a compelling justification, this Court) should adhere to directly controlling precedent rather than treating later doctrinal shifts as an implicit overruling, particularly in a complex, highly regulated area where reliance interests and institutional legitimacy are substantial. Petitioners’ assurance that other “guardrails” remain is both uncertain and not a basis for a narrow ruling, because the constitutionality of the coordinated-expenditure limits in FECA depends on the broader anticircumvention structure Colorado II already credited. Given available narrower grounds—simply applying Colorado II to uphold the statutory caps—stare decisis and minimalism counsel affirmance rather than reopening the contribution/expenditure framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: FECA’s caps on party committees’ coordinated expenditures, 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d), restrict core political speech and associational activity at the heart of the First Amendment, and the Constitution’s text contains no original-public-meaning basis for permitting Congress to ration such party–candidate advocacy based on an amorphous “anti-circumvention” theory. Treating coordinated party expenditures as “contribution-like” regulation dilutes the First Amendment by allowing Congress to evade strict scrutiny through labeling, a move in tension with Buckley’s central distinction between expenditures and contributions and with the Constitution’s limited grant of federal power. To the extent Colorado II, 533 U.S. 431 (2001), upheld these limits, it should be overruled because it lacks grounding in the First Amendment’s original meaning and permits broad prophylaxis untethered to the only historically cognizable corruption interest—quid pro quo. Petitioners are therefore entitled to relief from § 30116(d)’s coordinated party expenditure limits notwithstanding Colorado II.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps, 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d), are directly governed by FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II), 533 U.S. 431 (2001), which treated coordinated party spending as contribution-like and upheld these limits as a permissible anti-circumvention measure to protect candidate contribution limits and prevent quid-pro-quo corruption or its appearance. Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Express, 490 U.S. 477 (1989), lower courts (and ordinarily this Court absent a compelling showing) should follow controlling precedent rather than declare it implicitly overruled by later cases. Petitioners’ reliance on “guardrails” is practically unstable (as the argument itself suggests those guardrails may be contested), and eliminating the caps would invite circumvention by routing large donations through party committees for coordinated spending with candidates. Whatever later campaign-finance decisions say about independent expenditures, Colorado II’s core rationale about coordination functioning as a contribution remains materially applicable here, so I would adhere to stare decisis and uphold the statute.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps permissibly treat candidate-coordinated party spending as contribution-like, because coordination creates a direct risk of quid pro quo corruption or its appearance and enables circumvention of base candidate contribution limits—precisely the anti-circumvention rationale this Court accepted in Colorado II. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts (and this Court absent a compelling stare decisis basis) should follow directly controlling precedent rather than reweigh policy claims that later doctrine has shifted, particularly where petitioners cannot credibly assure that the “other guardrails” they invoke will remain to prevent evasion. As a pragmatic matter, removing the caps would predictably expand the ability of large donors to route influence through party committees closely aligned with candidates, burdening electoral fairness and undermining public confidence—harms that fall most heavily on voters with the least access and power. Accordingly, the coordinated party-expenditure limits do not violate the First Amendment on this record and should be upheld.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Colorado II directly upheld FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps by treating coordinated party spending as contribution-like and sustaining the limits as an anti-circumvention measure protecting the valid governmental interest in preventing quid pro quo corruption or its appearance. Under Rodriguez de Quijas, lower courts (and we, absent a genuinely distinguishable posture) should follow controlling precedent rather than treating later doctrinal shifts as an invitation to disregard it, especially where petitioners’ theory largely repackages the same coordination-as-contribution question Colorado II decided. Petitioners’ asserted “guardrails” depend on the continued force of other contribution limits they cannot commit to leaving undisturbed, which undermines the workability of striking these particular caps while keeping the statutory scheme coherent. Given FECA’s design to prevent donors from using parties as conduits to evade candidate limits, the coordinated-expenditure caps remain a permissible, targeted prophylaxis consistent with Colorado II’s anti-circumvention rationale.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps regulate spending made in concert with a candidate and thus function, in operation, like contribution limits aimed at preventing circumvention of candidate contribution caps—an anti-circumvention rationale this Court accepted in Colorado II, 533 U.S. 431 (2001). Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477 (1989), lower courts (and this Court absent a compelling stare decisis showing) should follow directly controlling precedent rather than treating later doctrinal “tension” as an invitation to disregard it. Petitioners’ arguments that coordinated party spending is more “speech-like” than “contribution-like,” and that the policy consequences would strengthen parties, do not overcome Colorado II’s core holding that coordinated expenditures present a quid-pro-quo and circumvention risk sufficient to justify limits under existing First Amendment doctrine. While the First Amendment concerns are serious, this case—framed as a challenge to the coordinated party limits alone—does not supply a principled basis to overrule Colorado II’s determination that coordination changes the constitutional analysis.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado II, 533 U.S. 431 (2001), squarely upheld FECA’s caps on party coordinated expenditures, treating coordinated party spending as “contribution-like” because it can function as an anti-circumvention backstop for candidate contribution limits and the quid-pro-quo corruption/appearance interest. Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/American Express, Inc., 490 U.S. 477 (1989), lower courts—and this Court absent a compelling stare decisis showing—should follow directly controlling precedent rather than treating later campaign-finance cases as impliedly overruling it. Petitioners’ request to revisit Colorado II rests heavily on contested policy predictions (about strengthening parties and “guardrails”), but stare decisis, institutional legitimacy, and the practical administrability of the contribution/expenditure framework counsel restraint where Congress has long relied on these prophylactic limits in 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d). Absent a clear doctrinal incompatibility or unworkability showing, I would adhere to Colorado II and uphold the coordinated-expenditure limits as a permissible anti-circumvention measure.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party-expenditure caps remain constitutional under this Court’s existing First Amendment framework because coordinated spending with a candidate is properly treated as contribution-like regulation aimed at preventing circumvention of valid contribution limits and quid-pro-quo corruption or its appearance. Colorado II directly upheld these same coordinated party expenditure limits on that anti-circumvention rationale, and under Rodriguez de Quijas lower courts (and this Court absent a principled stare decisis basis to overrule) should follow controlling precedent rather than treat intervening cases as silently discarding it. Petitioners’ reliance on later decisions such as Citizens United and McCutcheon does not squarely abrogate Colorado II’s holding about party-candidate coordination, and the continuing statutory structure of FECA (including base limits and anti-circumvention rules) makes this a classic context for respecting precedent to preserve doctrinal and methodological consistency. Given the narrow and party-specific nature of the regulation, and Colorado II’s determination that coordination functions like a contribution, petitioners have not shown sufficient justification to revisit that settled rule here.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FECA’s coordinated party expenditure caps, 52 U.S.C. §30116(d), regulate spending made in concert with a candidate and thus operate contribution-like for anti-circumvention purposes; Colorado II upheld materially the same limits under “closely drawn” scrutiny because coordinated party spending can be used to evade candidate contribution limits and foster quid pro quo corruption or its appearance. Whatever later campaign-finance decisions have said about independent expenditures, this case involves coordination, and under Rodriguez de Quijas lower courts (and absent a compelling stare decisis basis to depart) must follow directly controlling Supreme Court precedent rather than treat doctrinal drift as an implicit overruling. Petitioners’ practical “guardrails” argument is undermined by their inability to commit that other constraints will remain, and weakening an anti-circumvention measure risks real-world dilution of contribution limits that protect electoral fairness and public confidence. On this record, the coordinated limits remain a procedurally workable, narrowly targeted prophylactic rather than a broad suppression of party speech.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether FECA’s limits on coordinated party expenditures with federal candidates violate the First Amendment and whether (or how) the Court should revisit or distinguish FEC v. Colorado Republican Federal Campaign Committee (Colorado II), which upheld those limits against a facial challenge.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Campaign Act (FECA) coordinated party expenditure limits (the statutory caps on spending by national/state party committees that is coordinated with a candidate), challenged under the First Amendment (speech and association).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (party committees) argue that coordinated party expenditure limits burden core political speech and association by restricting parties’ ability to speak in concert with their own nominees, and that doctrinal developments in campaign-finance jurisprudence since Colorado II undermine its reasoning (especially its anti-circumvention rationale and treatment of coordinated spending as regulable like contributions). They contend the limits distort the system by pushing money toward outside groups and away from accountable political parties, and that other existing contribution limits and disclosure rules provide sufficient anti-corruption and anti-circumvention guardrails even if coordinated-party caps are removed. They also press that even if Colorado II rejected a facial challenge, an as-applied route (or a renewed facial challenge in light of later cases) should be allowed because the legal landscape and evidentiary predicates have changed.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (FEC and aligned parties) argue Colorado II squarely controls because it already upheld these coordinated-party limits on the ground that coordinated expenditures are functionally equivalent to contributions and may be capped to prevent circumvention of candidate contribution limits and resulting quid pro quo corruption risks. They emphasize that lower courts must follow directly applicable Supreme Court precedent (Rodriguez de Quijas) and that relabeling the same theory as 'as-applied' cannot evade stare decisis when the factual and legal premises are materially the same as those Colorado II considered. Respondents further argue that removing coordinated-party caps would open a major circumvention channel (large donors routing funds through parties to benefit specific candidates), and they dispute the claim that striking the limits would necessarily strengthen parties or improve democratic accountability.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the most serious point: that “anti-circumvention” risks becoming an unbounded rationale to suppress core political speech, especially after our cases cabined “corruption” to quid pro quo. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Colorado II’s holding is narrower than that critique suggests—it treats spending coordinated “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” with a candidate as contribution-like precisely because it functions as a conduit for candidate-specific value and thus directly protects the integrity of valid base limits. Justice Gorsuch is right that Rodriguez de Quijas is not an excuse for us never to revisit precedent, but under a minimalist stare decisis approach we should not overrule a directly controlling, coordination-specific decision absent a clear doctrinal collision or demonstrated unworkability, neither of which petitioners have shown on this record. I would therefore affirm on narrow grounds limited to coordinated party expenditures and without extending Colorado II beyond that setting.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kagan’s central point—invoking Colorado II plus Rodriguez de Quijas to preserve stability in FECA—does not answer the antecedent First Amendment question: whether the Constitution’s text and original public meaning permit treating a political party’s coordinated advocacy with its own nominee as “contribution-like” speech that may be capped on a generalized anti-circumvention theory. Even accepting Buckley’s categories, the coordination label cannot itself transform core political advocacy into a regulable “transfer” absent a concrete quid pro quo corruption risk; later cases narrowing “corruption” to quid pro quo (as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes) expose Colorado II’s functional-equivalence/balancing approach as doctrinally and historically unmoored. Justice Alito’s conduit concern highlights that earmarking and actual pass-throughs can be targeted directly, but it proves too much: it would justify broad suppression of coordinated party speech whenever Congress hypothesizes donor routing, a rationale the First Amendment’s original meaning does not license. Because Colorado II rests on an ahistorical premise that conflicts with the First Amendment’s protection of political speech and association, stare decisis alone cannot justify continuing to enforce § 30116(d) against coordinated party expenditures.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas make the best doctrinal point that our later cases have tightened “corruption” to quid pro quo and cautioned against layered prophylaxis, but that critique does not squarely negate Colorado II’s narrower, coordination-specific holding that expenditures made “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” with a candidate are contribution-like and regulable to prevent circumvention of valid base limits. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Rodriguez de Quijas counsels adherence to controlling precedent where later “drift” does not make the prior holding unworkable or doctrinally impossible, and I do not see that level of conflict here because coordination is precisely where quid pro quo risks and conduit dynamics are most concrete. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning objections are serious, but accepting them would require overruling (not distinguishing) Colorado II, and petitioners have not supplied the kind of strong stare decisis justification—beyond first-principles disagreement—that would warrant that step in this statutory scheme. Practically, eliminating § 30116(d) would predictably facilitate routing large, candidate-directed support through parties, weakening Congress’s contribution-limit structure in ways our cases have long recognized as a legitimate anti-circumvention concern in the coordination context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that our more recent campaign-finance cases narrow “corruption” to quid pro quo and caution against layered prophylaxis, but that critique does not squarely reach Colorado II’s coordination-specific premise: when the party spends “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” with the candidate, the spending becomes contribution-like because it can deliver candidate-directed value and directly threatens the integrity of valid base limits. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Rodriguez de Quijas and stare decisis have special force in election-law regimes where Congress calibrated interlocking rules, and petitioners’ “as-applied” framing largely repackages the facial challenge Colorado II rejected without a materially distinct record showing unworkability. Justice Thomas’s originalist objection usefully warns against free-floating anti-circumvention rationales, but here the line is administrable and concrete (coordination), and invalidation would predictably expand a conduit that disproportionately amplifies large-donor access at the expense of voters with fewer channels of influence. I therefore would adhere to Colorado II on its narrow terms and uphold § 30116(d) without extending the rationale beyond coordinated expenditures.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s best point is that our later cases tighten “corruption” to quid pro quo and caution against “prophylaxis-upon-prophylaxis,” which—if this were an independent-expenditure limit—would be powerful. But Colorado II’s coordination-specific premise fits within even that narrowed framework because coordination is the mechanism by which donors can deliver candidate-directed value through a party, making circumvention of valid base limits concrete rather than speculative. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that, under Rodriguez de Quijas principles, we should not treat doctrinal drift as silently overruling a directly controlling holding embedded in FECA’s interlocking scheme absent a showing of unworkability or direct inconsistency, which petitioners have not supplied on this record. Justice Thomas’s original-meaning critique would require us to overrule Colorado II outright; given the statute’s text treating spending “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” as distinct, and the administrable coordination line, I do not see a sufficient legal basis to do so here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s stare decisis point—echoed by Justices Kagan and Kavanaugh—that Colorado II is “directly on point” and Rodriguez de Quijas counsels adherence is the best argument for affirmance, but it does not answer the antecedent constitutional question whether Colorado II’s contribution-equivalence premise remains compatible with our later, stricter understanding of “corruption” as quid pro quo rather than generalized influence or layered prophylaxis. Coordination may make speech more effective, but under the First Amendment’s text and our post-Colorado II cases, effectiveness and access are not corruption; to sustain a direct cap on a party’s coordinated advocacy, the government must show a concrete quid pro quo risk, not an abstract “conduit” theory untethered to bribery-like exchange. And while Rodriguez de Quijas properly instructs lower courts not to anticipate our overrulings, it does not obligate this Court to preserve a precedent whose rationale has become doctrinally incoherent; if Colorado II truly compels the result here, we should confront whether it should be narrowed or overruled rather than extend its anti-circumvention logic. Administrability concerns Justice Kagan raises cannot justify diluting core political speech where narrower tools (base limits, earmarking rules, and disclosure) directly target quid pro quo without capping coordinated party-candidate advocacy as such.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that our post–Colorado II cases tighten “corruption” to quid pro quo and caution against “prophylaxis-upon-prophylaxis,” potentially leaving Colorado II looking overbroad. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Colorado II’s holding is coordination-specific: when spending is made “in concert” with the candidate, it operates as a conduit for candidate-directed value and thus fits within the quid-pro-quo channel those later cases preserve, rather than relying on generalized anti-distortion or mere appearance. Under an institutionalist, stare decisis-forward approach (and the Rodriguez de Quijas discipline Roberts invokes), I do not see a direct doctrinal collision or unworkability showing that justifies overruling an on-point precedent in an interlocking election-law scheme. Petitioners’ “as-applied” posture still targets the core rule that coordinated party expenditures are contribution-like, and without a materially distinct factual record, the Court should affirm narrowly without extending Colorado II beyond coordinated expenditures.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s originalist objection is the strongest counterweight: that the First Amendment’s text does not confer a general “anti-circumvention” power and that coordinated party advocacy looks like core expenditure speech. But Colorado II’s holding is narrower and more text-adjacent than that characterization suggests: it treats spending made “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” with a candidate as contribution-like because coordination is the mechanism that converts spending into candidate-directed value, implicating the quid-pro-quo channel our later cases still recognize. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize under Rodriguez de Quijas, petitioners’ position largely requires overruling (not distinguishing) Colorado II, and Justice Gorsuch’s “doctrinal drift” point does not establish a direct incompatibility that makes Colorado II unworkable on this record. I therefore adhere to precedent and uphold § 30116(d) without extending Colorado II beyond coordinated expenditures.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest point—that later cases narrowing “corruption” to quid pro quo and warning against “prophylaxis-upon-prophylaxis” (as Justice Gorsuch echoes) undercut Colorado II—does not, for me, defeat the coordination-specific premise that spending made “in cooperation, consultation, or concert” can operate as a conduit for candidate-directed value and thus be treated as contribution-like. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, Rodriguez de Quijas principles and stare decisis weigh heavily where a directly controlling precedent structures an interlocking election-law regime; petitioners’ proposed alternatives (base limits, earmarking rules, disclosure) read as policy substitutions rather than a doctrinal incompatibility that makes Colorado II unworkable. On a progressive pragmatic view focused on procedural fairness and practical consequences, the coordination line remains administrable and meaningfully preserves political speech by leaving parties free to make unlimited independent expenditures while preventing predictable circumvention of valid candidate contribution caps. I therefore do not see a genuine legal undermining of my rationale sufficient to change my vote.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado II, 533 U.S. 431 (2001), directly upheld FECA’s coordinated party expenditure limits on the grounds that coordinated spending is “functionally equivalent to contributions” and may be capped to prevent circumvention of valid candidate contribution limits and the attendant risk of quid pro quo corruption or its appearance. Under Rodriguez de Quijas v. Shearson/Am. Express, 490 U.S. 477 (1989), lower courts (and prudentially this Court absent a compelling showing) should follow controlling precedent rather than treat later doctrinal drift as an invitation to discard it, especially in a complex, highly regulated federal statutory scheme where institutional stability matters. Petitioners’ arguments about changes in the campaign-finance landscape and asserted benefits to party strength go to policy and legislative-fact disputes; they do not justify overruling Colorado II on this record, and a narrow disposition respecting stare decisis best preserves the Court’s legitimacy. I would therefore affirm the coordinated-party caps as a permissible anti-circumvention measure within FECA’s contribution-like regulation framework recognized in Colorado II and related cases (e.g., California Medical Ass’n v. FEC, 453 U.S. 182 (1981)).
